title: How do you start preparing for case interviews from scratch?
description: Everything you need to start preparing for case interviews, in order: how cases work, the ten stages, frameworks, maths, sizing, fit and a study plan.
hook: Start by learning how a case flows from opening to recommendation, then build the core skills one at a time (structuring, maths, charts, market sizing and fit) and practise full cases out loud as early as you can. You do not need a business degree or a stack of books. This guide puts everything in order, shows you a complete first case, and points you to the page on this site for each step.
body:
In this guide

  • Step 1: understand what you are preparing for
  • Step 2: learn the ten stages of a case
  • Step 3: work through the course
  • Step 4: learn frameworks without memorising them
  • Step 5: build maths, charts and sizing
  • Step 6: prepare for the fit interview
  • Your first full practice case
  • Mistakes beginners make in preparation
  • Pick a plan for the time you have
  • Check yourself

Step 1: understand what you are preparing for

A case interview is a conversation, usually 20 to 40 minutes, about a realistic business problem. You are not expected to know the answer. You are expected to break the problem down, use numbers sensibly and reach a clear recommendation, talking the interviewer through your thinking as you go. Most interviews also include questions about your experience, and these can count as much as the case. If this is all new, read what a case interview is and what interviewers look for first. It takes ten minutes and frames everything below.

Step 2: learn the ten stages of a case

Almost every case follows the same arc. Learn it once and no case will feel shapeless again.

  1. Listen and take notes: everything later links back to the goal you write down now.
  2. Recap: shows you listened and checks you are solving the right problem.
  3. Clarify: three questions at most. The right one can split the case in two.
  4. Structure: your plan for the whole case, and the skill interviewers weigh most heavily.
  5. Lead the case: propose the next step yourself instead of waiting to be told.
  6. Charts and exhibits: find the one thing that matters and say what it means.
  7. Maths: turns opinions into evidence. Work out loud and sanity-check.
  8. Brainstorm: "what else could the client do?" is a structuring question in disguise.
  9. Recommend: the last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers and writes up.
  10. Throughout: you are judged on how you come across in every minute.

When you want the exact words for each stage, keep what to say at each stage of a case beside you.

Step 3: work through the course

The free PrepForCase course is eleven lessons of about ten minutes each. Do them in order; each builds on the last.

  1. How case interviews work: the two formats and the six scored skills.
  2. The opening: listen, recap and clarify in the first three minutes.
  3. Structuring: issue trees, MECE and saying where you would start.
  4. Driving the case: steering, summarising and linking back to the goal.
  5. Case maths: approach first, round smartly, check everything.
  6. Charts and exhibits: a five-step routine for turning any chart into an insight.
  7. Market sizing: the structure earns the points, not the final number.
  8. Brainstorming: buckets, not lists.
  9. The recommendation: answer first, reasons with numbers, risks, next steps.
  10. How you come across: voice, composure and business fluency.
  11. The fit interview: six to eight stories that cover most questions.

Step 4: learn frameworks without memorising them

Most cases fall into three families: diagnosing a problem (profits are down), deciding yes or no (should we enter, buy, invest) and generating options (how can we grow). Each family has a few standard shapes. Which framework to use for each type of question covers the eleven that handle nearly every case.

The point of learning them is to recognise the shape quickly, not to recite boxes. Interviewers notice instantly when a structure would fit any company. A good structure uses this client's words: for a bakery, "ingredients, staff, rent" rather than "variable costs, fixed costs".

Step 5: build maths, charts and sizing

Case maths is percentages, growth, margins, break-even and a few more. The case maths cheat sheet has every formula on one page. Charts come next: one chart a day in the chart drill, with the insight said in one sentence, builds the skill quickly. For estimation questions, read the market sizing guide and then work through the 24 worked examples.

Ten minutes of mental maths a day beats a two-hour session once a week. Use the speed maths drill and say every step out loud.

Step 6: prepare for the fit interview

Half of most consulting interviews is about you. Start with the fit questions firms ask most, then build six to eight stories using the fit interview guide. One good story about leading a team through a setback can answer three or four different questions. Rehearse each out loud until you can tell it in about two minutes.

Your first full practice case

Do this once you have read the first three lessons. The aim is not to perform perfectly; it is to complete the loop of structure, evidence, calculation, implication, recommendation on your own.

The prompt: "A neighbourhood café's profit has fallen even though sales are steady."

  1. Recap and clarify. "Profit is down, sales are flat. Is the goal to restore last year's profit? Are other cafés nearby seeing the same?" Assume the answer is yes, and no.
  2. Structure. Profit = revenue − costs. Revenue is flat, so your hypothesis is that costs rose. Split costs into ingredients, staff, rent and delivery and packaging.
  3. Evidence. Revenue stayed at $1M. Costs rose from $850k to $900k, so profit fell from $150k to $100k: down $50k, or one third.
  4. Calculation. Suppose the cost lines are: ingredients $300k to $340k, staff $350k to $355k, rent flat at $150k, delivery and packaging $50k to $55k. Ingredients rose $40k, which is 80% of the $50k increase and a 13% rise on last year's ingredient bill.
  5. Implication. "Ingredients explain most of the fall. Next I would check whether that is supplier prices or waste."
  6. Recommendation. Suppose milk and coffee bean prices rose. "Recover the $50k by renegotiating with suppliers or switching one, and test a small price rise on drinks. A 5% price rise on $1M of sales is $50k if volume holds, so even a smaller rise plus supplier savings would close the gap. The risk is losing regulars to the chain down the road, so test it in the quiet hours first."

Then score yourself: where did you hesitate, and what would you say differently? Repeat the loop on a new case from the casebook until the sequence feels natural.

Mistakes beginners make in preparation

  • Reading instead of practising. You cannot learn cases by reading about them, any more than you can learn to swim from a book. Start speaking cases out loud in week one.
  • Memorising frameworks. A recited framework sounds recited. Learn why each branch exists so you can adapt it.
  • Only doing full cases. Full cases are slow feedback. Short drills on structure, maths and charts fix specific weaknesses faster.
  • Leaving fit to the last week. Stories take time to find, shape and rehearse. Start them early.
  • Fixing everything at once. After each case, write down the one thing to fix next time, and only that. The full list is in the most common case interview mistakes.

Pick a plan for the time you have

  • One week to go: a day-by-day plan focused on your biggest gaps.
  • Three weeks: the usual run-up, building week by week.
  • Six weeks or more: for starting from zero, with time to build real skill.

If you are new to business altogether, read preparing without a business background as well.

Check yourself

1. A friend says they will start practising cases once they have finished reading two books. What would you tell them?

Show the answer

Start now. Read the first three course lessons, then do a case out loud this week. Reading builds vocabulary; only practice builds the skill of thinking and talking at the same time.

2. In the café case, the interviewer says costs were flat at $850k and revenue fell to $950k. What is the profit, and where do you look next?

Show the answer

Profit is $950k − $850k = $100k, the same one-third fall. Now the problem is revenue, so split it into number of customers × average spend, and by time of day or product, to find where the $50k went.

3. Which three stages of a case do beginners most often skip practising?

Show the answer

The opening (recap and clarify), leading the case and the recommendation. They practise structuring and maths and then lose easy points at the start and end. Rehearse openings and 60-second closes on their own.
